abstract: A Federal Reserve Board FEDS Note by Paul E. Soto, Mason Thieu and Jeffrey S. Allen presenting publicly available indicators that researchers and policymakers can use to track the generative AI buildout and its economic impact on a timely basis. The indicators are organised into three categories that follow the sequence usually associated with general-purpose technologies: capabilities and costs; firm investment and adoption; and productivity and labor. The note is a measurement and data-infrastructure contribution rather than a source of new estimates, and it is explicit that the absence of a large aggregate signal in 2026 is consistent with, rather than evidence against, meaningful future productivity effects, because adoption remains shallow.
keyFindings: Organises AI tracking indicators into three sequential stages: capability improvements and cost declines precede broad firm adoption and investment, which in turn precede measurable aggregate productivity gains and labor market outcomes.

Headline firm adoption figures overstate real usage: they "do not reflect usage intensity, which surveys suggest remains shallow even where reported adoption is broad." Census BTOS adoption trends upward with a generally positive association between adoption and firm size.

"The absence of a large aggregate signal as of 2026 would not necessarily invalidate future productivity impacts, given the shallow adoption outlined in the previous section." Historically, measured productivity gains from general-purpose technologies lag investment by years.

Productivity gains do not translate proportionally from task to firm: "A 10% improvement on a task does not necessarily lead to proportional gains for a firm if adjustment costs or other bottlenecks lie elsewhere in the production process."

Recommends tracking sectoral productivity split by AI exposure level, unemployment and labor force participation for workers aged 20-24 against prime-age workers aged 25-54, and layoffs, discharges and job openings within information-processing sectors as a white-collar displacement signal.

Cites Korean semiconductor export prices as a useful proxy for AI input costs, given that Samsung and SK Hynix account for roughly 70 percent of global DRAM supply and dominate high-bandwidth memory production.

Characterises early labor evidence as operating through hiring rather than separations, citing Lichtinger and Hosseini Maasoum that AI is affecting younger workers via slower hiring rather than outright layoffs.
methodology: Descriptive compilation and documentation of publicly available time series, accompanied by a downloadable data file. Indicators span model capability benchmarks (including the time-horizon of software engineering tasks LLMs can complete 50 percent of the time), semiconductor and compute input costs, Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey adoption by firm size on a four-period moving average of biweekly data, an investment-accounting decomposition of AI-related contributions to GDP that down-weights net exports by the capital-goods share of imports, quarterly labor productivity by industry exposure group, and standard CPS and JOLTS labor series disaggregated by age and sector.
qualifiers: This note contains no new causal estimates and no original survey. Its empirical content is a curated set of existing public series, and the labor and productivity literature it cites (Bick et al., Brynjolfsson et al., Crane and Soto, Handa et al., Lichtinger and Hosseini Maasoum) is already tracked in this corpus, so it should not be double-counted as independent evidence. Figures are presented without 95 percent confidence intervals. The note is explicitly agnostic on the direction of future effects and frames the current absence of an aggregate signal as uninformative about the long run, so it supports a neutral rather than directional reading. Value here is as a methodological reference for which series to monitor.
